claims.text: At fixed noble-metal composition, thermal dwell time near the melting or decomposition temperature governs crystal-structure selection through the balance between element-specific diffusion and nucleation kinetics.
A longer high-temperature dwell increases atomic mobility.
A longer dwell permits partial equilibration among the noble-metal precursors.
Partial equilibration reduces localized compositional fluctuations and increases elemental-distribution uniformity.
Extending the dwell produces a more homogeneous single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle rather than phase-separated or segregated structures.
A longer dwell slows heterogeneous nucleation.
A longer dwell minimizes rapid local supersaturation of faster-diffusing elements.
Diffusion equilibration suppresses phase separation and unwanted secondary phases.
A longer dwell will improve particle-morphology control relative to the short-dwell baseline.
Rapid-heating and rapid-cooling protocols typically yield phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology in the stated nanoparticle regime.
The controlled experiment holds composition and peak temperature constant while varying dwell time.
The proposed intervention applies to noble-metal compositions containing more than five elements under rapid heating followed by quenching.
The useful dwell-time window is limited by nanoparticle growth and agglomeration.
Kinetic control is applicable when constituent melting and diffusion properties are sufficiently similar.
A transient temperature near 1100 K is typical of the relevant synthesis regime.
Element pairs with strongly disparate diffusion coefficients or melting points may remain incompletely homogenized despite an extended dwell.
The optimal dwell duration for balancing equilibration against growth or agglomeration is unknown.
Failure of longer dwell times to produce a statistically significant improvement in phase purity, elemental homogeneity, or morphology would falsify the hypothesis.
